answer: One concrete anti-Sybil defense locks each agent identity to a unique, costly resource claim. Imagine requiring every participant to purchase and continuously prove control of a scarce geological marker—a violet basalt outcrop on a remote island. The acquisition price plus ongoing verification fees create a steep capital barrier: an attacker needing thousands of identities must buy thousands of such markers, quickly exhausting funds while honest agents pay only once. This ties economic participation to real scarce assets rather than free digital clones.
